summary: This program keeps a list of farmers' market products and uses Java streams to answer questions about them: which organic summer items are cheapest, which vendors are present (now sorted alphabetically with duplicates removed), and what one vendor sells (now capped at three lines).

lines.text: Comparator supplies the ready-made ordering objects that sorted() needs when you want to sort by something other than natural order, such as a product's price.
Collectors holds the recipes that turn a finished stream back into an ordinary collection; every method here ends with Collectors.toList().
All of the stream work below flows from this one list, so it is created first even though the book leaves the filling-in of items to you.
A reminder that the list starts empty: until you add products, every stream result printed below will be empty too.
The main method stays short by delegating each question to its own static helper, which is the pattern the rest of the class follows.
The name still says "Set" but the return type is now a List, because the requested change was an alphabetically ordered result and a plain set has no order.
Storing the vendor name in a variable means the same value drives the menu lookup, the heading, and the discount calculation.
forEach with a method reference prints each menu line on its own row, which reads better than printing the list's bracketed form.
This call is the next piece of work: the matching helper is still only a comment at the bottom of the class, so you must write it before the program will compile.
stream() opens a pipeline over the list; nothing actually happens until a terminal operation such as collect() runs at the end.
filter keeps only the products that pass this test, and the null check on the season guards against a NullPointerException before toLowerCase is called.
Sorting happens while the elements are still MarketProduct objects, so the price is available to order by even though only names come out at the end.
map replaces each product with its name, turning a stream of products into a stream of strings.
The terminal operation that runs the whole pipeline and gathers the results into a new List.
The vendor pipeline maps first, so the remaining steps deal with simple strings rather than whole products.
Products with a missing or empty vendor are dropped so they cannot appear as blank entries in the printed list.
distinct removes repeated vendor names, giving the uniqueness a Set would have provided.
Called with no argument, sorted uses the natural order of String, which is the alphabetical ordering the exercise asked for.
equalsIgnoreCase lets "baker's lane" match "Baker's Lane", so a difference in capitalization does not hide a vendor's products.
This commented-out line shows where alphabetical sorting would go if you wanted the first three menu items chosen by name rather than by list position.
Each product becomes one display string, and String.format("%.2f", ...) pins the price to two decimal places so it reads like money.
limit stops the pipeline after three elements, satisfying the request to show at most three menu items.
